questions.question: What is 'Denial of Wallet' in the context of autonomous agents?
options: An attacker stealing an agent's API keys to run up a bill
An agent loop generating spend with no cap to stop it, running unbounded until the budget is exhausted
A billing policy that blocks agent API access after a spending threshold
A security vulnerability where agents can forge payment requests
questions.explanation: Denial of Wallet describes an agent that keeps reasoning, keeps tool-calling, and keeps billing with nothing designed to stop it. The loop is the failure mode, not an external attack. The real-world case: an e-commerce agent's monthly cost jumped from $1,200 to $4,800 after a new tool created an unbounded polling loop.

questions.question: What is a 'velocity limit' and which failure mode does it specifically address?
options: A per-request token cap that limits how fast the model generates tokens
A per-minute or per-hour spend rate limit that catches runaway loops faster than monthly caps—fires within minutes when an agent enters a tight spending loop
A limit on the speed at which agents can be deployed
A rate limit on the number of parallel agent sessions
questions.explanation: A velocity limit is a spend cap per short time window (e.g., $50 in 10 minutes). It catches runaway loops (a tight 5-second retry loop burning tokens) before monthly caps fire. A single monthly cap would not trigger until the wallet is largely gone.

questions.question: Why is a layered cost-governor stack better than a single cap at one time scale?
options: Single caps are not supported by cloud provider billing APIs
Different failure modes operate at different time scales: runaway loops caught by velocity limits, slow leaks by daily caps, bad releases by weekly/monthly caps
Single caps require more complex code to implement than layered caps
Regulators require at least three distinct cap levels for production AI systems
questions.explanation: A single monthly cap catches a runaway agent only after the wallet is gone. A single per-request cap catches nothing at the session level. Runaway loops need velocity limits; slow leaks need daily caps; bad releases need monthly caps. The stack covers failure modes at appropriate time scales.

questions.question: What does 'tiered model routing' accomplish as a cost-governor primitive?
options: It routes different tasks to different cloud regions based on cost
It defaults to a cheaper smaller model and escalates to a larger model only when a classifier judges the task warrants it
It batches multiple small requests into one large model call to reduce overhead
It splits long contexts across multiple model calls to stay within token limits
questions.explanation: Tiered routing defaults to a smaller, cheaper model and escalates to a larger one only when a classifier judges the task warrants it. This cuts cost significantly for the large fraction of agent steps that do not require frontier-level reasoning.

questions.question: What key principle does the lesson derive from the real $1,200 to $4,800 cost increase case?
options: Every new team member should review agent billing monthly
Every new tool surface is a potential new loop, and every new tool needs its own per-tool cap and per-tool alert
Agents should be limited to one tool at a time to prevent cost surprises
Monthly billing audits are sufficient to catch all agent cost failures
questions.explanation: The real case: a new order-tracking tool allowed the agent to poll during every session with no per-tool cap or alert. The fix was a per-tool cap plus a daily-growth alert. The lesson: every new tool surface is a new potential loop and needs its own cap and its own alert.

questions.question: Claude Code's `max_budget_usd` fires on session aggregate cost. What does the lesson recommend combining it with?
options: A manually checked weekly billing review
A velocity limit enforced externally (spend per short window) plus explicit tool allowlists and per-tool caps
Disabling all tools except file writes to keep costs predictable
Using only the cheapest available model to prevent budget overruns
questions.explanation: max_budget_usd fires on session aggregate—it catches bad releases and prolonged slow leaks but not a tight loop that burns $50 in 10 minutes. A complementary external velocity limit catches the loop-based burn. Tool allowlists and per-tool caps address new-tool-surface risk.
